newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Karachi seen voting on ethnic lines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Karachi seen voting on ethnic lines.

text.p: After years of bloodshed, Karachi's ethnic divisions are likely to decide how the city's 12 million people vote in Monday's elections, analysts say.
All the contestants are preaching ethnic tolerance at their election rallies, but most are counting on the "ethnic vote".
Most people in Pakistan's biggest city and commercial hub tend to identify with parties seen as having roots in the city's Mohajir, Sindhi, Pashtun, Punjabi or Baluchi communities.

"No one has worked for alleviating the misery we live in, so there is no difference between the candidates," said taxi-driver Mohammad Amin. People, he added, should therefore stick by candidates from their own communities and hope for the best.
Few Karachi'ites believe the elections will herald an end to recurring ethnic, sectarian and political violence that took about 500 lives last year and more than 2,000 in 1995.
Mohajirs, Urdu-speaking Moslems who left Hindu-majority India when Pakistan was formed in 1947 at the end of the British Raj, form a majority of the sprawling port city's population.
Mohajirs have often been at odds with Karachi's other ethnic groups, including Sindhis, Pashtuns, Punjabis and Baluchis.
Thousands of people have died in years of often ferocious unrest in Karachi as the Mohajir National Movement (MQM) fought against what it saw as discrimination against Mohajirs.
Though the violence has cooled in recent months, bitter memories of a crackdown launched by the ousted government of Benazir Bhutto are fresh in the minds of all the ethnic groups.

The MQM believes it can get vengeance at the polls, winning most of the city's 13 National Assembly seats, but Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) is hoping that the result in one electoral contest will vindicate its iron-fist policy.
The PPP has fielded former interior minister Naseerullah Babar as its candidate in NA-184, a marginal seat.
Babar, the man Mohajirs love to hate, will be fighting against candidates from the MQM and Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML), as well as political newcomer Imran Khan.
The constituency is in Baldia Town, about half of whose residents are Mohajirs. The PPP won it in 1988, the MQM in 1990 and the PML in 1993, when the MQM boycotted national elections.
"Babar is a favourite among the Punjabi, Pashtun, Sindhi and Baluchi voters for his action against the MQM," said Abdul Qadir Patel, a former PPP provincial assembly member.

Nazim Haji, provincial chief of Imran's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement), said Pakistan's former cricket captain would do well. "It is hard to break the MQM's Urdu-speaking vote-bank but a lot of Pashtuns and Punjabis may opt for Imran," he said.
Political observers say Imran has little chance to win the seat, but he and the PML incumbent could dent PPP support.
The only Karachi seat the PPP is seen as sure to win is Lyari, a slum constituency dominated by ethnic Baluchis, where the party has won in every election since 1970.
